title: How Body Armor Works: A Special Request
summary: Josh and Chuck answer a special request from a soldier named Donald Anderson, deployed in Iraq, asking how modern body armor works. They trace body armor history from animal hides and tree bark through chain mail and metal plates, then explain soft Kevlar vests (woven fiber layers, tight weave distributing bullet impact, bullet-resistant rather than bulletproof), hard ceramic plates (alumina, stopping rifle rounds), and shear thickening fluid (STF) liquid body armor using silica particles in polyethylene glycol. They discuss blunt force trauma from armor, future materials like Vectran, goat-produced spider silk, and feather-based cloth from Nebraska researchers. The episode closes with listener mail suggesting the mouth/cheek and buttocks as good places to get shot, and thanks to listeners in the military.

segments.title: Opening and special request from a soldier
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode as a special request from Donald Anderson, a soldier in Iraq who wrote in asking how body armor works, and explain why they took the request.

segments.title: History of body armor
segments.summary: Early body armor was made from animal hides and tree bark, then metal such as chain mail. Gunpowder made metal armor obsolete because bullets pass through metal plates.

segments.title: Soft Kevlar vests and terminology
segments.summary: Modern soft vests are made of Kevlar, a DuPont fiber about five times stronger than steel by weight. The hosts note that bullet resistant is more accurate than bulletproof, and that Kevlar is a brand name. Tightly woven layers spread the impact across the vest, like a soccer goal net or a tight tennis net.

segments.title: Hard ceramic plates
segments.summary: Hard armor uses ceramic plates, such as alumina, that are very hard and do not shatter. They stop rifle rounds, while soft vests stop pistol rounds. Many soft vests have pockets for inserting plates. The plates are thick, so they are worn mainly when a threat is expected.

segments.title: Liquid body armor and shear thickening fluid
segments.summary: Shear thickening fluid (STF) is made of silica particles suspended in an oily liquid, such as polyethylene glycol. On impact the particles lock into a rigid shield within milliseconds, then return to a flexible state. Tests reportedly needed four Kevlar layers with STF to match fourteen plain layers, and STF has moved into production. Police officers may avoid heavy vests, so comfort matters.

segments.title: Blunt force trauma and future materials
segments.summary: Armor must not give like a net, or the force can cause internal damage and shock waves. Armor makers use dense weaves. Future materials mentioned include Vectran, about twice as strong as Kevlar, spider silk from genetically engineered goats, and cloth spun from chicken feathers by Nebraska researchers.

segments.title: Listener mail on best places to get shot
segments.summary: The hosts read listener suggestions for where to get shot: William Hartel, a St. Louis dentist, describes a cheek wound that missed teeth, and Lewis from North Carolina suggests the buttocks, avoiding the pelvic nerves. The hosts thank listeners and the soldier, and sign off.
